title: Cinematography basics
text: Chapter 03 Cinematography basics. A monitoring app is only useful if you know what you are looking at. This chapter explains the ideas behind every tool in the app, in the order you meet them on a shoot. Each section ends with the tool that handles it. title: Exposure: how much light reaches the sensor
text: Exposure is the amount of light the sensor records. Too little and the image is dark and noisy. Too much and bright areas clip , which means they turn solid white with no detail that can be recovered later. Three camera settings control exposure, and they interact, which is why people call them the exposure triangle.

title: Aperture (f-number)
text: The aperture is the opening inside the lens. A low f-number such as f/1.8 is a wide opening: more light and a shallow depth of field, so the background blurs. A high f-number such as f/11 is a small opening: less light and more of the scene in focus. Each full stop ( f/1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16 ) halves the light. Cinema lenses are often marked in T-stops, which are f-stops corrected for the

title: Shutter speed and shutter angle
text: The shutter sets how long each frame is exposed. In video there are two ways to express it. Shutter speed is a fraction of a second, such as 1/50 . Shutter angle is borrowed from film cameras, where a rotating disc with an opening of a certain angle exposed each frame. A 180° angle means the frame is exposed for half of the frame interval. At 24 fps that is 1/48 s; at 50 fps it is 1/100 s. The rea

title: ISO, base ISO and dual base ISO
text: ISO is the sensor's amplification. Raising it brightens the image but also amplifies noise. Every sensor has a native (or base) ISO where it delivers its best balance of noise and dynamic range. Many modern cinema sensors have two base ISOs, for example a low base around 800 for daylight and a high base around 6400 for low light. At each base the sensor runs a different analog gain and is cleanest

title: Exposure compensation and metering
text: In an automatic exposure mode the camera's meter picks the exposure. Exposure compensation nudges that decision brighter or darker in thirds of a stop. Metering mode decides which part of the frame the meter trusts: the whole frame (matrix), the centre, a small spot, or the highlights so they are protected. In manual mode (M) the meter only advises; your settings decide. In the app The Mode , Expo

title: Frame rate and slow motion
text: Frame rate is how many pictures per second the camera records. 24 fps is the cinema standard; 25 fps is used for television in 50 Hz countries and 30 fps (29.97) in 60 Hz countries. Recording at 50, 60, 100 or 120 fps and playing it back in a 24 or 25 fps project gives slow motion: 120 fps played at 24 fps is five times slower than life. Two frame rates matter: the sensor (or capture) rate, which

title: White balance, Kelvin and tint
text: Light sources have a colour. Candlelight is orange, midday sun is neutral, open shade is blue. White balance tells the camera what should look white. It is expressed as a colour temperature in Kelvin : around 3200 K for tungsten lamps, 5600 K for daylight, 6500 K or more for shade. Setting a lower Kelvin makes the image bluer; a higher Kelvin makes it warmer. Tint is the second axis, shifting betw

title: Log, Rec.709 and HLG: why the picture looks flat
text: A sensor captures far more brightness range than a normal screen can show. The camera has to squeeze that range into the file. Rec.709 (standard video) does it by throwing away the extremes: it looks finished straight out of the camera, but highlights clip early and the shadows are crushed. Log profiles instead compress the range with a logarithmic curve that keeps every stop the sensor captured.

title: LUTs: looking at log through a lens
text: A LUT (look-up table) is a file that maps every input colour to an output colour. A technical LUT converts a log image to Rec.709 so it looks normal on a monitor. A creative LUT adds a style on top: a film emulation, a bleach bypass, a warm teal-and-orange look. On set a LUT is for monitoring : the camera still records the flat log file, and the LUT only changes what you see on the phone. That is

title: Reading exposure with scopes
text: Scopes are graphs of the picture. They do not care how the screen is set or how bright the room is, which makes them the only trustworthy way to judge exposure in log. The app offers four, and two overlay tools that paint the result straight onto the image.

title: IRE, code values and middle grey
text: Scopes measure brightness in IRE , a 0 to 100 scale where 0 is black and 100 is the brightest value the file can hold. Under the hood the file stores 8- or 10-bit code values (0 to 255 or 0 to 1023). Two landmarks matter. Middle grey is an 18% reflectance card, the reference for a correctly exposed scene. In Rec.709 it sits around 40 to 45 IRE; in N-Log around 35 IRE; in Log3G10 around 33 IRE. Cli

title: Histogram
text: A histogram counts how many pixels sit at each brightness, dark on the left, bright on the right. A pile-up against the right edge means clipping; against the left edge, crushed shadows. It is fast to read but it does not tell you where in the frame the problem is.

title: Waveform
text: A waveform plots brightness vertically against horizontal position in the frame, so a bright window on the right of the picture appears as a bright spike on the right of the scope. It is the cinematographer's standard tool: you can read the level of a face, a sky or a wall directly. The app draws guide lines for clip, highlight, middle grey and shadow at the right levels for the current log curve,

title: RGB parade
text: Three waveforms side by side, one for red, green and blue. When the three traces line up for a neutral object the white balance is right. If the blue trace sits higher than the others on a grey wall, the image is too cool. The parade is the best tool for matching white balance between cameras.

title: Vectorscope
text: The vectorscope ignores brightness and plots only hue and saturation. The centre is grey; distance from the centre is saturation; the angle is the hue. Six boxes mark the standard colour-bar targets, and a diagonal skin line shows where all human skin tones fall regardless of ethnicity. If a face sits off the skin line, the white balance or tint is wrong.

title: Zebras
text: Zebras paint diagonal stripes on the parts of the picture that reach a chosen level. Classic use: highlight zebras at the clip point, so stripes mean "this is gone". The app also offers zebras for middle grey, so you can put stripes on a grey card or a face and know it is at the right level, and for crushed shadows.

title: False color
text: False color replaces the whole picture with a colour per exposure band: purple for crushed black, blue for deep shadow, green for middle grey, pink for skin, yellow and orange for highlights, red for clipped. It is the fastest way to see the exposure of everything in the frame at once. Different cameras and apps use different palettes, so a legend is always shown.

title: Exposure lights and posts
text: When the whole scope is too much, a summary helps. X-Lights are three lamps per channel that turn on as highlights or shadows get close to the limit. X-Posts are two meters, one for clipping pressure and one for noise, that you can glance at while watching the picture. They are the "traffic lights" of exposure: green means fine, amber means close, red means act. In the app All of these are in Live

Protect the highlights Turn on highlight zebras or false color and bring the brightest thing you care about just under clip. title: Focus
text: A small phone screen makes focus hard to judge, and in video a missed focus cannot be fixed later. Two kinds of help exist. Focus peaking outlines the sharpest edges in a colour, so you can see what is in focus without zooming. Punching in magnifies part of the frame so you can check critical focus on an eye. Peaking is quick and works while rolling; punch-in is precise but you lose the overview.

title: Framing, aspect ratios and anamorphic
text: The sensor records one shape (usually 16:9 or 3:2) but you may deliver another: 2.39:1 widescreen cinema, 1.85:1 , 4:3 , or vertical 9:16 and 4:5 for social platforms. Frame guides draw the delivery shape over the picture, and a matte darkens the area outside it, so you compose for what the audience will see. Safe areas are inset borders that keep action and titles away from edges that some screen

title: Codecs, RAW and bit depth
text: The codec is how the camera compresses the video into a file. H.264 and H.265 (HEVC) make small files that play anywhere but tolerate less grading. ProRes 422 HQ is lightly compressed, large, and the editing standard. RAW formats ( N-RAW , ProRes RAW , R3D ) store the sensor data before white balance and much of the processing, so those decisions can be changed in post. RAW files need a compatible

title: Audio levels
text: Digital audio is measured in dBFS (decibels relative to full scale), where 0 dBFS is the loudest value the file can hold. Unlike analogue tape, there is nothing above 0: a peak that hits it is clipped and distorts. Dialogue is usually recorded with peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS, leaving headroom for surprises. The camera meters show the current level and hold the peak for a moment so you can see wha

title: Timecode
text: Timecode is a clock stamped on every frame, written as HH:MM:SS:FF . Editors use it to line up picture with separately recorded sound and to sync multiple cameras. Rec Run timecode only advances while recording, so each clip continues from the last. Both are for exposures longer than the camera's longest timed shutter, typically for astrophotography or light painting.
